newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Murdoch too removed to comment-Australia's PM.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Murdoch too removed to comment-Australia's PM.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard hit back on Thursday at criticism from media magnate Rupert Murdoch, saying he was too removed from Australia to comment.
"I think the remarks Rupert made indicate just how disconnected he's becoming with Australia," Howard told Australian Broadcasting Corp radio.

"Anybody who has been in Australia over the past few months, particularly the past couple of months and has really followed things closely, could barely say that we haven't achieved some quite fundamental reforms."
On Wednesday in an interview with Australian Broadcasting Corp television, Murdoch warned Australia was in danger of becoming a backwater unless the government began a far more radical reform agenda.
He specifically mentioned the need for industrial relations and tax reform, and repeated his belief that gun law reform and the racism debate had distracted the government.

"I was fascinated by his comment that we were distracted by the guns debate," Howard said. "Yes, I was. I plead guilty to that. I think the Australian public wanted me to be distracted by that. They, in fact, didn't regard it as a distraction."

Howard also denied that Australia had been subjected to a racism debate, claiming that controversy in the past three months over immigration levels was a response to Independent politician Pauline Hanson's first speech to parliament.
During that speech in early September, Hanson warned Australia was in danger of being swamped by Asians.

"We've not had a race debate -- we've had a debate about responses to a speech -- and nobody in the government, nobody in the opposition, nobody is seriously arguing that we should go back to the White Australia policy," Howard said.
"I've made it very clear that under no circumstances is that going to happen," he said.
However, he said the level of Australia's non-discriminatory immigration intake was a subject for legitimate debate.
Howard's radio interview was promoted as an end-of-year review for the conservative Liberal-National government, which was elected to office on March 2.
